title: Soil properties and laboratory tests
summary: Almost every numerical question in this subchapter can be answered from one relation, e·S = w·G, plus the definitions of the phase ratios. Learn that equation and the three-phase diagram, and the rest follows by algebra rather than memory. The remaining questions are laboratory facts: which test, which apparatus, which standard number of blows or layers. The Atterberg limits and the two Proctor tests are examined every sitting, and the classification system (IS 1498) rewards understanding the A-line rather than memorising symbols.

sections.heading: The three-phase system and the phase relations
sections.body:
Soil is a **three-phase** material — **solids, water and air**. Every phase relation is a ratio of volumes or weights drawn from that diagram.

| Quantity | Definition | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Void ratio e** | **V_v / V_s** | Referred to the volume of **solids**, so it **can exceed 1** |
| **Porosity n** | **V_v / V** | Referred to the **total** volume, so it **never** exceeds 1 |
| **Degree of saturation S** | V_w / V_v | 0 dry, 1 (100%) fully saturated |
| **Water content w** | W_w / W_s | By **weight of solids**, so it can exceed 100% |
| **Air content a_c** | V_a / V_v | = 1 − S |
| **Percentage air voids n_a** | V_a / V | = n · a_c |

> **e = n/(1 − n)**  and  **n = e/(1 + e)**

**The master equation** — commit this one to memory and derive the rest:

> **e · S = w · G**

For a **fully saturated** soil S = 1, so **e = wG**. This single relation, with the definitions above, answers virtually every phase-relation problem set in the examination.

**Unit weights:**

| Unit weight | Expression |
|---|---|
| Bulk (moist) | γ = (G + Se)γ_w /(1 + e) |
| **Dry** | **γ_d = γ/(1 + w)** = Gγ_w/(1 + e) |
| Saturated | γ_sat = (G + e)γ_w/(1 + e) |
| **Submerged (effective)** | **γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w** = (G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e) |

The **dry unit weight** is the key measure of compaction, because it removes the effect of water and measures how much **solid** has been packed into a unit volume.

**Relative density (density index)** for coarse-grained soils:

> **I_D = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min) × 100%**

| I_D | State |
|---|---|
| 0 – 15% | Very loose |
| 15 – 35% | Loose |
| 35 – 65% | Medium |
| 65 – 85% | Dense |
| 85 – 100% | Very dense |

Note the inversion: **a high relative density means a LOW void ratio**. It applies to sands and gravels; for clays the equivalent descriptor is **consistency index** or **liquidity index**.

**Specific gravity of solids G** is **2.65 – 2.70** for most soils, determined by the **pycnometer (density bottle)**. Organic soils are lower; soils rich in iron minerals higher. **Take G = 2.65 when none is given.**

sections.heading: Index properties and the Atterberg limits
sections.body:
The **Atterberg limits** mark the water contents at which a fine-grained soil changes state. In **descending** order of water content:

> **liquid limit > plastic limit > shrinkage limit**

| Limit | Meaning | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **Liquid limit (LL)** | Soil begins to flow as a liquid | **Casagrande** apparatus, **25 blows**, groove closing over **12 mm**; or **cone penetrometer**, 20 mm in 5 s |
| **Plastic limit (PL)** | Soil ceases to be plastic and crumbles | Rolled into a **3 mm thread** which just crumbles |
| **Shrinkage limit (SL)** | Further drying causes no further volume reduction | Mercury displacement |

**The derived indices:**

> **Plasticity index PI = LL − PL**
> **Shrinkage index SI = PL − SL**
> **Liquidity index LI = (w − PL)/PI**
> **Consistency index CI = (LL − w)/PI**
> **Flow index** = slope of the flow curve; **Toughness index = PI / flow index**

**PI = LL − PL**, not LL − SL. That single substitution is the most frequent error in the subchapter.

**What PI means physically:** it is the **range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically**. A high PI means a large range, hence a highly plastic clay:

| PI | Description |
|---|---|
| 0 | Non-plastic (sand) |
| < 7 | Low plasticity |
| 7 – 17 | Medium plasticity |
| > 17 | High plasticity |

**Activity = PI / (% clay fraction finer than 2 micron)** identifies the clay mineral: **kaolinite ≈ 0.4–0.5** (inactive, stable), **illite ≈ 0.5–1.0**, **montmorillonite ≈ 1.0–7.0** (highly active). Montmorillonite is the mineral responsible for **expansive (black cotton) soils** — it swells enormously on wetting and shrinks on drying, which is why it damages light structures and pavements.

**Sensitivity = undisturbed strength ÷ remoulded strength**, at the same water content. A **sensitive** clay loses most of its strength on disturbance, which is why undisturbed sampling matters and why driving a pile into such a clay temporarily destroys its capacity (recovered later by **thixotropy**).

**Grain size distribution** from **sieve analysis** (coarse fraction) and **hydrometer or pipette analysis** (fines, using **Stokes' law**):

> **Uniformity coefficient C_u = D_60/D_10**
> **Coefficient of curvature C_c = D_30²/(D_10 · D_60)**

**Well graded** requires **C_u > 6** for sand, **> 4** for gravel, and **C_c between 1 and 3** for both. A **higher C_u means a WIDER range of sizes**, hence better grading — the relation candidates most often invert. A well-graded soil compacts to a higher density because smaller particles fill the voids between larger ones.

**Effective size D_10** is the sieve size through which 10% passes; it correlates with permeability (**Allen Hazen: k ≈ C·D_10²**).

sections.heading: Soil classification — IS 1498
sections.body:
The **IS Soil Classification System** (essentially the Unified system) separates soils at the **75 micron** sieve:

| Group | Fraction | Symbol pattern |
|---|---|---|
| **Coarse grained** (> 50% retained on 75 μ) | Gravel **G**, Sand **S** | Second letter W, P, M or C |
| **Fine grained** (> 50% passing 75 μ) | Silt **M**, Clay **C**, Organic **O** | Second letter L, I or H |
| Highly organic | **Pt** (peat) | — |

**Second letters** for coarse soils: **W** well graded, **P** poorly graded, **M** with silt, **C** with clay. So **SW** is well-graded sand, **GC** clayey gravel.

**Second letters** for fine soils are **compressibility** by liquid limit — and note this is a **compressibility** classification, not a plasticity one:

| Symbol | Liquid limit |
|---|---|
| **L** — low | **LL < 35** |
| **I** — intermediate | **35 ≤ LL ≤ 50** |
| **H** — high | **LL > 50** |

So **CH** is a clay of high compressibility, **ML** a silt of low compressibility.

**The plasticity chart and the A-line** do the actual discrimination between silt and clay:

> **A-line:  PI = 0.73 (LL − 20)**

| Position | Soil |
|---|---|
| **Above** the A-line | **Clay (C)** |
| **Below** the A-line | **Silt (M)** or organic (O) |

There is also a **U-line, PI = 0.9(LL − 8)**, an upper bound above which no natural soil plots — a useful check that test results are credible.

**Why the A-line rather than grain size?** Because the **engineering behaviour of a fine soil is governed by its plasticity, not its particle size.** Two soils with the same grading can behave utterly differently depending on their clay mineralogy, and plasticity captures that where a sieve cannot. This is the single most important idea in soil classification.

**Particle size ranges (IS):**

| Fraction | Size |
|---|---|
| Boulder | > 300 mm |
| Cobble | 80 – 300 mm |
| **Gravel** | **4.75 – 80 mm** |
| **Sand** | **0.075 – 4.75 mm** (coarse/medium/fine) |
| **Silt** | **0.002 – 0.075 mm** |
| **Clay** | **< 0.002 mm** |

Note that **silt and clay are separated by size in the grading curve but by plasticity in the classification** — and the classification governs.

sections.heading: Compaction and the Proctor tests
sections.body:
**Compaction** is the **rapid densification of soil by mechanical energy, expelling AIR.** It must be kept apart from **consolidation**, which is the **slow expulsion of pore WATER** under load. The two are confused constantly:

| | **Compaction** | **Consolidation** |
|---|---|---|
| Expels | **Air** | **Water** |
| Speed | **Immediate** | **Slow** — months to years |
| Cause | **Mechanical energy** applied deliberately | **Applied load** |
| Applies to | Partly saturated soil, in **construction** | **Saturated clay**, in service |

**The two Proctor tests:**

| | **Standard Proctor** | **Modified Proctor** |
|---|---|---|
| Layers | **3** | **5** |
| Blows per layer | 25 | 25 |
| Rammer | **2.6 kg** | **4.89 kg** |
| Drop | **310 mm** | **450 mm** |
| Energy | ~600 kJ/m³ | ~2700 kJ/m³ — about **4.5 ×** |

**Greater compactive effort gives a HIGHER maximum dry density at a LOWER optimum moisture content.** The compaction curve shifts **up and to the left** — a result worth understanding rather than memorising: with more energy, less water is needed to lubricate the particles into a dense packing.

**The compaction curve** rises to a peak (the **maximum dry density** at the **optimum moisture content**) and then falls. It falls on the wet side because water begins to **occupy volume that solids could have occupied** — and, since air cannot be entirely expelled, the curve approaches but never reaches the **zero air voids line**:

> **γ_d(zero air voids) = Gγ_w/(1 + wG)**

That line is a theoretical limit, so a plotted point lying **on or above** it indicates a **test error**.

**Effects of compaction:** increased **shear strength** and **bearing capacity**, reduced **permeability**, reduced **compressibility and settlement**, reduced **swelling and shrinkage**, and increased resistance to **erosion and frost**.

**Field compaction plant, matched to the soil:**

| Plant | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Smooth wheeled roller** | Granular soils, finishing |
| **Pneumatic tyred roller** | Wide range, including bituminous work — kneading action |
| **Sheep foot (pad foot) roller** | **Cohesive** soils — kneading |
| **Vibratory roller** | **Granular** soils — rearranges particles |
| Rammer / plate compactor | Confined areas, trenches |

Matching the plant to the material is the difference between reaching target density and merely passing over the ground.

**Field density measurement:** **core cutter** (soft fine-grained soil) and **sand replacement** (gravelly or hard soil, where a core cutter cannot be driven without damage). **Relative compaction = field dry density ÷ laboratory maximum dry density**, specified as at least **95–100%** depending on the layer.

**Compaction is done on the DRY side of optimum for a permeable fill** and slightly **wet of optimum where low permeability is wanted**, as in an earth dam core — because wet-side compaction produces a **dispersed** structure of lower permeability, dry-side a **flocculated** structure of higher strength.

sections.heading: The laboratory tests, as a set
sections.body:
Each test measures one property, and knowing which apparatus goes with which property is worth several marks a paper.

| Property | Test / apparatus | IS 2720 Part |
|---|---|---|
| **Water content** | Oven drying at **105–110 °C**; also sand bath, alcohol, calcium carbide (rapid, field) | 2 |
| **Specific gravity G** | **Pycnometer / density bottle** | 3 |
| **Grain size** | **Sieve analysis**; **hydrometer** for fines (Stokes' law) | 4 |
| **Liquid and plastic limits** | **Casagrande** apparatus; 3 mm thread | 5 |
| **Shrinkage limit** | Mercury displacement | 6 |
| **Compaction** | **Standard / Modified Proctor** | 7, 8 |
| **Permeability** | **Constant head** (coarse) / **falling head** (fine) | 17 |
| **Consolidation** | **Oedometer (consolidometer)** | 15 |
| **Direct shear** | **Shear box** | 13 |
| **Triaxial compression** | **Triaxial cell** — UU, CU, CD | 11, 12 |
| **Unconfined compression** | UCS apparatus | 10 |
| **Vane shear** | Vane, laboratory or field | 30 / IS 4434 |
| **CBR** | 50 mm plunger at **1.25 mm/min** | 16 |
| **Field density** | **Core cutter** / **sand replacement** | 29 / 28 |
| **Free swell index** | For expansive soils | 40 |

**Choosing the permeability test.** **Constant head** for **coarse** soils, because the flow is fast enough to measure a steady discharge; **falling head** for **fine** soils, where the flow is too slow for that and the fall of head in a standpipe is measured instead. In the field, a **pumping-out test** gives a value averaged over a large mass, which is what actually matters for a dewatering or seepage problem.

**Choosing the shear test.** The **triaxial** test is the most versatile because it **controls drainage and can measure pore pressure**, so it yields either total or effective stress parameters as required. The **direct shear box** cannot control drainage and forces failure on a **predetermined plane**, which may not be the weakest. The **vane shear** test gives the **undrained strength of soft, sensitive clay in situ**, where an undisturbed sample cannot be recovered at all.

**Undisturbed sampling** matters because index tests can be run on disturbed material but **strength and consolidation tests cannot**. The measure of sample quality is the **area ratio**:

> **A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100%**

kept **below 10%** for an undisturbed sample (a thin-walled **Shelby tube**), whereas a **split-spoon** sampler in the SPT has an area ratio over 100% and returns only a **disturbed** sample. Also relevant are the **inside clearance** (0.5–3%, so the sample does not bind) and **outside clearance** (0–2%, to reduce driving friction).

**A discipline worth stating.** Laboratory tests are run on small specimens, while the soil mass in the field contains **fissures, laminations, root holes and variability** that no 38 mm triaxial specimen represents. That is why field tests (SPT, vane, plate load, pumping) are used alongside laboratory ones, and why soil parameters are always applied with judgement rather than as exact quantities.

formulas.label: Master phase relation
formulas.expression: e · S = w · G     (for saturated soil, e = wG)
formulas.note: Every other phase relation can be derived from this with the definitions of e, n, S and w.

formulas.label: Void ratio and porosity
formulas.expression: e = V_v/V_s ;  n = V_v/V ;  e = n/(1−n) ;  n = e/(1+e)
formulas.note: e is referred to solids and can exceed 1; n is referred to total volume and cannot.

formulas.label: Unit weights
formulas.expression: γ_d = γ/(1+w) = Gγ_w/(1+e) ;  γ_sat = (G+e)γ_w/(1+e) ;  γ′ = γ_sat − γ_w
formulas.note: Dry unit weight is the measure of compaction, since it removes the effect of water.

formulas.label: Relative density (density index)
formulas.note: High relative density means LOW void ratio. Coarse-grained soils only.

formulas.label: Atterberg indices
formulas.expression: PI = LL − PL ;  LI = (w − PL)/PI ;  CI = (LL − w)/PI ;  Activity = PI / (% < 2 μ)
formulas.note: PI = LL − PL, never LL − SL. Activity identifies the clay mineral.

formulas.label: Grading coefficients
formulas.note: Well graded: C_u > 6 (sand) or > 4 (gravel), with C_c between 1 and 3. Higher C_u = wider range.

formulas.label: A-line on the plasticity chart
formulas.expression: PI = 0.73 (LL − 20)     — above it clay (C), below it silt (M)
formulas.note: Fine soil behaviour is governed by plasticity, not particle size. U-line: PI = 0.9(LL − 8).

formulas.label: Zero air voids line
formulas.note: A theoretical limit the compaction curve approaches but never reaches. A point on or above it means a test error.

formulas.label: Area ratio of a sampler
formulas.expression: A_r = (D_o² − D_i²)/D_i² × 100%     — below 10% for an undisturbed sample
formulas.note: A split-spoon sampler exceeds 100% and gives a disturbed sample only.
